WESTERN NATURAL RESOURCES Mr. CLARK:
1.	Has an agreement been arrived at between the Dominion government and the province of Manitoba for the transfer by the former to the latter of certain natural resources within the boundaries of Manitoba, belonging to the Dominion of Canada?
2.	Have the people of British Columbia, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island an interest in the natural resources referred to in paragraph one hereof, and, if so, what is the interest of each province herein?
3.	Have the provinces of British Columbia, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island been consulted as to the terms upon which said natural resources will be transferred?
4.	Has the approval been received from any of the last mentioned provinces to the terms upon which a transfer shall be made, and if so, by whom has such approval been given?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: QUESTIONS
subtopic: HOLDERS OF RANK OF DEPUTY MINISTER
speechtext:
1.	No.
2.	So long as subsidies continue to be paid to the province of Manitoba, in lieu of the transfer to that province of its natural

resources, it is obvious that the people of British Columbia, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island have an interest therein.
Whether such interest would continue after the transfer of the resources in lieu of subsidy payments, and the discontinuance of such subsidy payments, is a matter which has not been made the subject of judicial determination.
In the event of a transfer of the natural resources being made on the above terms, if any province should feel that it has a claim arising therefrom that claim would have to be considered on its merits and should not be an obstacle to the settlement as to control of natural resources between the Dominion government and the government of the province of Manitoba.
3.	Answered by the answers to Nos. 1 and
2.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. GOOD TO AMEND THE CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the special privilege now given to Racing Associations under the Criminal Code of carrying on public gambling operations in connection with their race meetings is detrimental to the best interests of Canada and should be abolished.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, the motion is
seconded by Mr. Denis, the member for Joliette. The substance of this resolution is identical with that of the resolution presented by me two years ago. The question at once arises-and it is a question which I ought perhaps to anticipate and answer now-why am I bringing up the matter again this year? Those who were here last year will remember that I had the same resolution on the order paper last year, but owing to the fact that the government took private members' day very early in the session, the resolution was not reached at all. I am bringing it up this year for several fairly distinct reasons. In the first place, I am not very easily discouraged, I hope, by such a defeat as the motion had two years ago. I believe in following the well known motto: "If at first you don't succeed try, .try again," and so long as I am able I wish to advance this cause in whatever way I can. I shall consider it not only a duty but a privilege to do so. I propose therefore to give the House an opportunity of dividing on the question again, and I sincerely hope that every hon. member of the House will feel it his duty and his privilege to express himself on this resolution.
I want also to say that I believe there was a misunderstanding two years ago in regard to a certain matter brought up in this connection by the then Minister of Justice, Sir Lomer Gouin, and I wish to deal specifically with that particular point because I hope that I can put it in such a way that there will not be any further misunderstanding. I desire therefore in that connection to draw the attention of hon. members to an extract from the fMr. Marcile.]
Hansard of March 1, 1923, page 739, where in the course of his remarks on my resolution the then Minister of Justice said of me:
He quoted the Hon. Mr. Raney as his main authority, I would say, to justify his resolution.
I might comment just here to the effect that I did not quote Mr. Raney on that occasion as my chief authority. That, however is neither here nor there. Continuing-and this I would bring to the attention of the members particularly-he said:
I am not sure that I shall surprise the hon. member for Brant, but I may tell him this, that the Hon. Mr. Ranejr has never asked for any such amendment as the amendment my hon. friend now proposes to this House.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. GOOD TO AMEND THE CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext: When my hon. friend spoke of Mr. Raney was he referring to the then Attorney General of Ontario?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. GOOD TO AMEND THE CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Yes, to Hon. W. E. Raney, then Attorney General of Ontario. The hon. gentleman (Sir Lomer Gouin) went on to state that he had had correspondence with the Attorney General of Ontario in regard to a proposed amendment to the criminal code that had to do with the prohibition of the publication of racing information, and so on, and the correspondence is all here. Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to point this fact out to the House very definitely, and I hope there will not be any further misunderstanding ; Mr. Raney for years asked for the amendment which I am advocating. But he did not ask for it in this particular correspondence that he had with the Minister of Justice, for the very good reason that the matter was then before the House in the resolution I then had on the order paper, and because the proposal which I made in the resolution dealt with a different matter entirely from the question which Mr. Raney was taking up with the then Minister of Justice. These two mat-ters-the question of removing the special privilege which is now extended to racing associations and which is contained in sub-section 2 of section 235, and the question of forbidding the publication of racing information in our newspapers-are two entirely different questions. They are related of course to the one evil of gambling, but they are entirely different questions and should not by any manner of means be confused, and I hope that during the course of the present debate the two questions will be kept absolutely distinct.
I do not propose, Mr. Speaker, to repeat the argument of two years ago. The matter was very fully debated on that occasion, and

Race Track Betting
I consider that it would be quite needless to cover the ground again. I would, however, at this point desire to repeat the summary I then gave of the legislation dealing with this matter so as to refresh the memories of hon. gentlemen.
If we refer, therefore, at the outset, to the Revised Statutes of 1906 we find that subsection 1, of section 235, made it an indictable offence punishable by one year's imprisonment and a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars:
(a)	To use or knowingly allow premises to be used for betting.
(b)	To keep, exhibit, employ or knowingly allow to be employed thereon any betting device.
(c)	To become a stake holder, or
(d)	To record or register a bet on an election, race
or contest.
But by sub-section 2 these provisions were not to apply to bets between individuals or to those made on a race course of any incorporated racing association during a race meet. Now, there we have the indictment, if you like, under sub-section 1, and the exemption under sub-section 2. I referred two years ago to the very lengthy discussion which took place in 1910 in connection with the so-called Miller bill as a result of which there was an amendment, a compromise amendment, made to this section which re-enacted sub-section 1 of the foregoing section, and' added to the list of offences therein contained by making it an offence:
(a)	To engage in poolL-sel'ling, or book-making or the business of betting, or to make an agreement for the purchase or sale of betting privileges or of information intended to assist in betting.
(b)	To advertise, print, publish, exhibit, post up, sell or supply, etc., or offer to sell or supply such information.
(c)	To advertise, print, publish, exhibit, or post up any offer, invitation, or inducement to bet.
(d)	To sell, transmit, deliver, or receive any message relating to book-making, pool-selling or betting.
(e)	To aid or assist in the foregoing.
But- the application of sub-section 1 was further limited by adding to sub-section 2 the provision that sub-section 1 should not apply-and I hope hon. members will listen to this carefully-to book-making, pool-making, betting or wagering upon such race course provided that such race meetings are not continued for longer than seven days or occur oftener than twice a year on such race course.
There was a further amendment in the year 1912, two years later, which re-enacted the foregoing sub-section 2, as amended1, but. limited the racing associations therein defined to those incorporated before March 20, 1912, and to any incorporated after that date by act of parliament or of the legislature of any
province, and also for the first time permitted racing associations to sell information or privileges to assist in or enable the conduct-ting of book-making, pool-selling, or betting, and so on, during the actual progress of a race meeting.
As a result of these two amendments-one in the year 1910 and the other in the year 1912-there was a general tightening up of the law against the keeping of what were defined as betting houses, and a general loosening up of the law as it applied to racing associations. That, I think, is a fair statement of the effect of those amendments. Now, in the year 1917, I think it was, an order in council was passed, to which I referred two years ago, wiping out these two exemptions for the duration of the war and I think a year afterwards-I have forgotten the exact dates; at all events this particular special privilege was wiped out by order in council in 1917 which order in council lapsed in January, 1920. During those three years this practice was discontinued, and I outlined to the House two years ago the effect of that discontinuance during the latter years of the war and for a year or two afterwards. About that time also the so-called Rutherford commission was appointed to go into this whole matter and report. As a result of that report there was a further amendment to the statutes in 1920 which re-enacted the foregoing sub-section as amended-that is subsection 2-but limited the non-applicability of sub-section 1 to bets made on a race course through the agency of the pari-mutuel system, limiting the percentage which could be retained by a racing association out of the amount of any money paid or stake deposited with such association and of which it became the depository under the pari-mutuel system, and providing that the type of pari-mutuel machine should be approved by the Minister of Agriculture, and that he must be satisfied that a proper proportion of the gate receipts and of the percentage retained as above was given in purses for the horses racing.
The Statutes of 1922 made a few -minor changes in sections 227 and 235. Instead of the words "between individuals" parliament-inserted the words "'between not more than ten individuals." There was also a specific exemption of race track operations permitted by the 1920 amendment. Two years ago there were also some further minor amendments to the law in this respect. Chapter 41, section 6 of the statutes of 1923 made a minor amendment to subsection 2 in respect of the percentage of the total amount of the stake which could be retained.
Race Track Betting

Such is a summary of the law dealing with this matter from the year 1906 to the present time.
I should like next to mention to the House that during the last two years there has been a notable increase in the number of tracks on which this race track gambling is being carried on. There are two more tracks in British Columbia, two more in Manitoba and two more in Ontario; and I think, as hon. members will have noted from the newspapers, there has been a very distinct increase in the handbook evil which is largely based on the racing and betting that goes on at the race meets. I have received, since the matter was first presented to the House two years ago, a great many unsolicited expressions of approval and appreciation of my action taken on that occasion, and expressions also of a desire that the matter should be kept to the fore, and that the House should deal with it again. I do not think it necessary to read any of these; I have them in my hand, quite a bunch of them as you will see, which have come from various organizations and places throughout the country. I may say also, Mr. Speaker, that two years ago I went to the races at Connaught Park to get first-hand information regarding the details of the pari-mutuel system. I was very hospitably and cordially entertained by the management, and taken in behind the scenes, and everything was explained to me in great detail. I appreciated this opportunity, but I may say that what I learned has only deepened my conviction as to the tremendous menace and evils of this special privilege granted these associations and which I am now asking parliament to take away from them.
I have something further to say in this connection, but I think it would be well for me to reserve it until the conclusion of the debate. I therefore leave the matter for the present in the hands of the House.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. GOOD TO AMEND THE CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
The resolution moved by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. 'Good) is one which I find myself unable to support, for the reason that it does not correct the evil. We remember that two years ago the hon. member for Laurier-Outre-mont (Sir Lomer Gouin), then minister of Justice, introduced, and this House passed, a bill designed to correct the evil of handbook betting. This measure, we all remember, was thrown out by the Senate. The resolution as presented by the hon. member for Brant deals entirely with betting which takes place upon the race tracks in the Dominion of Canada. It does not in any manner curtail the practice of betting on race tracks out-

side of Canada. In the Toronto Globe of last Saturday, on the front page, I find a very interesting article, which they feature in regard to the intimated legislation as outlined or forecast by the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) in which he has intimated that he will at this session of parliament introduce a bill curtailing the evil of handbook betting. In that connection the Toronto Globe of Saturday says:
Inspector Raises Both Hands for Anti-Handbook Measure
Staff Official of Toronto Police Department Declares 90 Per Cent of Illegal Traffic Would Disappear Immediately Proposed Amendment Became Law.
An Effective Blow at Elusive Evil
If passed by parliament, the amendment to the Criminal Code to be presented to the House during the present session by Hon. Ernest Lapointe, Minister of Justice, will practically wipe out handbooking, according to Staff Inspector David McKinney of the Morality Department of the Toronto police force. While it may not meet entirely with the spirit of the resolution passed at the Chief Constables' convention in Vancouver in 1922, the amendment will be of great assistance to the police of the Dominion in suppressing the handbook, the inspector added, in an interview yesterday.
Hits at Base of Supply
The amendment which will be presented by the Minister of Justice would make a person guilty of an indictable offence who advertises, prints, publishes, exhibits, posts up, sells or supplies, or offers to sell or supply, other than on the premises of an association lawfully conducting race meetings in Canada, and during the actual progress of a race meeting thereon, any tips, selections, odds, winning money prices, pari-mutuel payments, or any similar intelligence with respect to or applicable to any horse race, whether such race be held within or without the Dominion of Canada.
There are some quotations here from the city of Hamilton as follows:
Representative clergymen and police officials here agree that legislation prohibiting the publication of betting odds will go far toward eradicating the handbook evil. Some of them said to-day the traffic quickly would collapse once such a law were enforced effectively.
Chief of Police David Coulter said: "Suppress the information, and the entire handbook evil collapses. People are not going to wager money on something they can find out nothing about. I have always advocated reformers going after legislation to this effect."
Rev. Dr. J. L. Alexander, First Congregational Church: "Suppress the information, and you take the nerve out of the tooth. Everybody knows, especially those sporting writers who may be affected, that it is the publicity given their writings which keeps the public interest up. Suppression of the racing tip and odds will go far to put the bookmaker out of business."
That shows, I think, that public opinion is very largely behind the attempt to put the handbook out of business in Canada. I pick up the morning paper published in Ottawa, -and I find that, while there are to-day no

Race Track Betting
races being held in Canada, because at this season of the year, the race tracks are not operated, yet we find in all the principal daily papers of Canada there are three columns published of results of racing, and the morning paper says:
Racing on Three Tracks Miami, New Orleans, Tia Juana
Now, surely the people of Canada have very little interest in the races being held away down in Tia Juana, Mexico. We have sporting events in this country. For instance when a hockey match takes place, the reporters are in the arena and write up every detail of t!he game as it proceeds. People who follow hockey as a sport get a very fair idea as to how the game is played. When a boat race takes place, the newspapers devote a great deal of space to detailing every feature of the race, and although we sit at home, we can practically visualise the contest from start to finish. The same is true as regards every other contest and sporting event throughout the world. Therefore, in the report of a horse race, we would like to see the race detailed so that one could get some information in regard to the quality of each horse and where he is placed; but I am fairly satisfied that the publication of the news as it appears in the racetrack sheets is only for the purpose of carrying on handbook betting as it is carried on in this country. The sheet I hold in my hand is dated February 28, and in it is a list of results, which I will not detail, of the races of that date and then appear the entries for Monday. The details of the races which took place on the 28th give a complete list of the horses, the winners and also the also-rans. You would wonder why they print this in detail. People in this country are not very much interested in regard to races that take place outside of Canada, and I am satisfied that the object in view in printing this detailed information is that this is corroboration of exactly how the races went, so that those who won or lost their money have in this an authoritative report of what took place. There is a complete list for all three tracks outlining the activities that will take place there to-day, and to-morrow's paper will contain detailed information as to what horses won and what horses lost.
Before I take my seat, I hope to move an amendment which will attempt, at least, to correct this evil. The evil to-day is not that of the race-track as conducted in Canada. The crying evil that we have to-day is the practice of handbook betting. This amendment will, I hope, put out of business the resorts throughout Canada in which this trade and practice is carried on.

Derby day and the other great races in England have become English institutions. Lord Rosebery, in his younger days, made three prophecies. He said that he would at some future time be Prime Minister of England; that he would marry the wealthiest woman in England ; and that he would win the English Derby. He accomplished all of those three prophecies. He won the Derby three times: in 1894 with Ladas, in 1895 with Sir Vista, and in 1905 with Cicero. We find that while Lord Rosebery succeeded in winning the Derby on three occasions, the Prince of Wales has also accomplished that feat. maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. GOOD TO AMEND THE CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no apology whatever to offer in supporting the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good). The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork) has advocated the ancient and honourable sport of horse racing. As I understand the resolution, the legislation we are asking for has nothing whatever to do with horse racing, outside of the feature of gambling. We are dealing with the gambling feature, not with racing or the testing of speed of horses, and this resolution if adopted by this parliament will not interfere with horse racing as a sport; will not interfere with the raising and breeding of pure-bred horses; will not interfere with any of our local horse racing affairs; but it will interfere with the system that is now in vogue of gambling through the pari-mutuel machines at the meets that are held from time to time.
To my mind this resolution is of the utmost importance because it reaches down to the very root of our national life. We are building up a young nation in this country. We boast of our natural resources, of our great manufacturing industries, of our vast potential wealth, and rightly so; but the greatest asset this country has is its young men and young women, and if we are going to build up a strong country we must build on the foundations of morality and honesty and industry. This practice of gambling is one that will to a great extent mar the morals of our young men and our young women, and lead them off into channels that are not the best for the development of their manhood and their womanhood. We are trying to safeguard the youth of our land in asking for this legislation. We safeguard by legislation the pedestrians as they walk by the way; we safeguard the traffic on the public highway; we safeguard, to some extent, the industries of our country; we safeguard our homes by providing police protection: but particularly should we lay stress, more than we have in the past, on safeguarding the youth of our land. To those who are grown up in years, to hon. members in this parliament possibly, it might not make such a great deal of difference whether they gamble or not; but it will make a difference in the character, in the outlook, and in the honesty possibly, of many of our citizens, the young men and the young women who are growing up and helping to build up this great nation.
We have behind this movement, Mr. Speaker, I believe the united forces of the great majority of the organized churches in this country. I believe that the vast majority of all organizations for moral reform in this Dominion are behind the movement, and we should take cognizance of that fact knowing that they are the organizations that have built up this country. There is nothing that has done so much to build up this country to what it is to-day as the Christian forces that have been at work in Canada. We owe our intellectual, moral and social progress largely to the Christian churches that are founded on the word of God. It is related that on one occasion Queen Victoria was asked upon what rested the great success of the British Empire, and she pointed to the word of God. Now, believing that we have behind us the vast majority of the Christian organizations, in my opinion we should support this legislation, which will cut out this evil.
The question might be asked, what does gambling accomplish? In the first place, we might note some things that gambling does not do. I believe in healthy sports; I believe in field sports that will develop the physical energies and powers of our young men and young women; I believe in every organization that will develop the intellectual forces of our youth. But what does gambling do? Does it develop our physical forces? Does it develop our mental forces? Does it develop our moral forces? Does it develop us into more honest and better citizens? Does it help to make us more energetic and more active in connection with the affairs of our country? It does not require much cleverness to bet on horses, or to engage in other forms of gambling. As for the results which follow from gambling they do not contribute to the elevation of human beings from a physical, moral or intellectual standpoint.
And what is the effort which underlies gambling? It is the effort to get something for nothing. When we seek to obtain money through the agency of gambling we endeavour to obtain profit through some other individual's loss and our exertions are not likely to benefit the community in the same way that they would if they were directed toward some laudable purpose. An individual who used a room in a house for gambling purposes, and collected a rakd-off ostensibly to meet the cost of light or heat would be acting illegally and in the event of detection would become liable to the pains and penalties of the law. I remember a case of this kind which occurred not so very long ago. In that in-

Race Track Betting
tance the man used a certain room for gambling purposes and eight or ten men were caught there by the officer of the law. They were all brought before the court and fined. But why discriminate between one form of gambling and another? Why allow men to gamble on race courses when they are not allowed to gamble in gaming houses or in houses used for that purpose? If there is a form of gambling which is a menace to the entire community it is that which takes place on race tracks, and it would be in the national interest to make a clean sweep of all forms of gambling at once rather than to pass piecemeal legislation. I want to say that gambling creates thieves. I do not mean to say by any means that every individual who gambles is likely to develop into a thief; but there are numerous cases where men have not only spent the money which should have gone to the support of their wives and families, but also money which they stole from the tills of their employers. Let me read you some quotations along that line. Here is one from the Christian Guardian of January, 1924:
Only a few days ago in Toronto we had a case of a trusted official of the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment stealing 525,000 of the funds entrusted to him and losing it in gambling on horse races. Just a few days later in the same court we had two employees of the city registry office plead guilty to the theft of about $10,000 in one case and $4,500 in the other, and the money all went on the horses.
And not very long ago we read in the public press where a bank manager in the city of Hamilton had confessed to spending his all on horse racing and then had' gone to the bank till and drawn out thousands of dollars -I believe the amount was approximately $60,000-and he said it had all gone on the horse races. It was also reported in the newspapers quite recently that Mr. Jones, a police magistrate in Toronto, referring to bookmaking had said: it was the hardest form of evil that the police of that city had to cope with. Permit me to read a further quotation illustrating the waste of money which occurred in gambling. This is the opinion of a Mr. Burgess, who is identified with an insurance company. He says:
It has been my opinion for a great many years that the most serious cause of loss to fidelity companies through the dishonesty of employees in positions of trust is the gambling instinct engendered and fostered by the handbooks," he declared. " Nothing has caused the downfall of trusted employees more than the handbook. Fidelity losses were never so serious, and the one outstanding cause is the race track and the evils it creates in the shape of the handbook.
This particular evil has to do with handbooks, but all these forms of gambling are in-421
terwoven, and all should be swept out of existence.

speechtext:
No, it would not do away with the pari-mutuel. It would do away with the handbook as I understand it. I am pleased to note that the Minister of Justice is introducing legislation along that line. I commend him for his action. Such legislation was passed two sessions ago and thrown out by the Senate. We are delighted to have it before us again. It is a step in the right direction, but in my judgment it does not go far enough. In order to make it effective you have to go further. If you want to kill a rattlesnake, do not kill him piecemeal, but take his head off and get rid of him entirely. This race track gambling is an economic waste, and there is no question about it. We have in our country at the present, time many unemployed. There may be among those many who have wasted their money. If you go into restaurants when races are being held across the river you get in touch with young men and women and hear them say "I was over at the races, I was betting and lost so much money". It is a common occurrence, no matter where you go in this city or any other city where horse races are being conducted, you will hear individuals stating that they have been at the races and they have lost or won money. Money going into the pari-mutuel machines is an economic waste, because there is no tangible evidence that you are getting anything for your money, and very often people get so fascinated with it that they lose their all, and lose what belongs to somebody else in a great many
cases. I have a statement from Dr. Shearer which shows the staggering amounts which are annually wagered at the Canadian racing meets. The figures are:

In Ontario last year the sum wagered was $36,000,000. If $36,000,000 in the province of Ontario, or $80,000,000 in the Dominion of Canada goes to some place where you received no tangible or adequate return or reward in any way to benefit anybody, it is surely an alarming economic waste.
I wish to refer to another quotation that I have here, from Social Welfare, of Toronto:
Only in Mexico and Canada and three of the forty-eight American states is such criminal vice allowed by law. When it was driven out from under the Stars and Stripes it found refuge under the good old Union Jack in Windsor, Fort Erie, Vancouver and Victoria. How long shall Canada tolerate this?
In my experience in my younger days I laboured for some time in the United States. I returned to Canada, why? Not because I could make more money, because I was making a great deal more money in the United States at that particular time than I could make in this country; but I returned to Canada because of the British law which was so much better than the law of the United States. At that particular time we heard it currently stated that when the blacklegs, gamblers and thieves committed crime in Canada they went across the line in order to get more freedom in the United States. But things have changed since. Mexico, Canada and three of the states of the union are the only countries where it is permitted. We find forty-five of the states of the union are free from this gambling vice. We ought to realize that we are not advancing morally along lines of protecting our people against these vices as rapidly as our American cousins to the south of us are advancing.
In conclusion I wish to express my approval of the legislation that the Minister of Justice is bringing forward, and I hope this House will take into consideration the necessity of going further and putting all gambling into the same category. If it is illegal in one place to gamble, then make it illegal in every other place, and eradicate completely this form of gambling in this fair Dominion of ours.

speechtext:
I cannot help, on rising to make my
first speech in this House, but refer to the death of the late member for Northumberland, Mr. Morrissey, whose place in this parliament I was elected to fill. It was a pleasure to me to listen to the remarks made in reference to the hon. member by our respected leader on this side of the House (Mr. Mackenzie King), by the right hon. leader of the opposition, and the hon. leader of the Progressive party. Mr. Morrissey was a politician who stood high in the estimation of the people, a man who died with his name unsullied. Although he had

been for years at the head of the largest spending department of the local coalition government of which he was the only Liberal member, a government which later passed out under the blackest cloud that ever darkened the horizon of any government in New Brunswick. Mr. Morrissey's election in 1921 by the largest majority ever given a federal candidate in the county of Northumberland was a mark of personal esteem.
With these remarks dealing with the late member, I am glad that a moral issue of this nature is the one on which I make my first speech.
I would be [DOT] thoroughly in accord with the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork) if, in the amendment he introduced, he had left out the last few words, "unless applied on a race-track in Canada during a race meet." I feel that his amendment would be even more sweeping than the resolution moved by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good), and one that would have commended itself to me, if he had left out these qualifying words.
I am not opposed to horse racing; in fact, I am very much in favour of all sports. I am interested in horse racing, in race tracks, and in the fact that horse racing Should be kept clean from all those things that make it so obnoxious to many people that they are afraid to allow their boys and gills to go and see what should be clean sport. I feel that gambling and betting are insidious evils and perhaps as hurtful to the public mind and the young people especially of our country as is the drink habit. We have prohibited gambling at country fairs and in many other ways we have tried to restrict it, but I feel that we have strained at a gnat and swallowed a camel. We should go the whole length in this matter; we should try to protect the youth of this country from an evil as insidious as this great gambling evil is. We, who are further advanced in life, have seen some of the evils that have followed gambling. We have seen embezzlement; we have seen suicide, as was mentioned by one hon. member, and we have seen imprisonment and homes broken up. We, who are the legislators of this country, should legislate for the protection of our people against such a crying evil as gambling on the race tracks of this fair Dominion of ours. An hon. member who was speaking the other day in regard to another question referred to betting on an old sorrel horse. I do not wish, nor do I think any of those who have spoken against gambling, wish to restrict the right of any person attending a race track individually to bet five dollars or fifty dollars or fifty cents, as is referred to, except that I feel

Race Track Betting
that is one of the insidious things whereby young people who have started gambling in that way might be induced to gamble even worse than that. If, however, we restrict gambling to individual gambling, I do not think we shall have from it the bad effects that are produced as it exists at the present time.
The hon. member who has just sat down (Mr. Woods) referred to the fact that horse race betting is prohibited in the United States except in three states; yet we find that in this fair Dominion of ours, adjoining their borders, we are allowing race tracks to be operated under the pari-mutuel, handbook and other betting principles. This reminds me very much of a parent who forbids his children to carry on some evil habit, something that is wrong, while his neighbour on the other side of the fence encourages his children to carry on just the evil that is being prohibited, and to induce, if' possible, the other children to be corrupted by that method. We, as a great family living to the north of the boundary line should co-operate with our good friends to the south in doing everything we can to put out of this country forever the great gambling habit. I do not want to speak at any length on this question. I want to see gambling put off the race tracks. I want to see race tracks so clean that the best men, ministers of the gospel, every person, can go to see what I consider one of the finest sports and the greatest exhibitions we have in any country. I have visited our race tracks and I have gone across the Atlantic and have seen racing as it is carried on in the Old Country. I do not think Lord Rosebery or the king or anyone else raced their horses under the inducement that we do on many of the tracks in this country, where we know that jockeys are corrupted; that the 5 p.m. best horse does not always win;
and that under the influence of the betting, the gambling, a horse that is not entitled to the race is very often the winner. That sort of thing should be opposed vigorously by this House. We should stand in the best interest, not only of our young people, but of one of the best sports we have in this country and one that has been promoted since the time of Charles II in the Old Land, a sport that everyone could enjoy seeing. We do not want it to be surrounded by men who come in with handbooks mostly from across the border. The sum of $60,000,000 was mentioned. I should like to know where the great bulk of that $60,000,000 goes. Does it remain in Canada, or is it carried across the border by men who have been driven out of the United States by the laws they have there,
and who have come to corrupt our morals? Are they carrying back to that country money that belongs to our hard-working citizens, our clerks, artisans and other workers? Is that where we want the earnings of Canadians to go when we are struggling as we are to advance our country? Do we want to see that money, frittered away in that frivolous manner, carried across the border by men who are not entitled to the protection .that we give them in this land?
I feel very strongly in favour of supporting the amendment if the hon. member (Mr. Stork) would eliminate the last few words. I hope the day will come when the resolution as introduced to-day by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) will be carried, and when the other resolution is brought down by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), I hope to be able to support it. Then, we as Canadians can hold up our heads beside our neighbours to the south and say that we have grappled with the great evil of gambling.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. GOOD TO AMEND THE CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in at least one respect I find myself entirely in accord with one expression of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork), who moved the amendment, and that is when he says that horse racing is an ancient and honourable sport. Let us, in the first place, get clearly before our minds the subject now under discussion. It is not the desire of the mover or of any of those who are supporting his resolution to do away with the noble animal, the race horse, in this country,
Race Track Betting

neither is it the purpose or desire of any of us to prohibit horse racing in Canada. Personally, I enjoy watching a good horse race just as much as anybody else, and in my younger days I enjoyed having the privilege, which I did have many a time, of riding one of those noble animals at the races-I want to qualify that,-races where public gambling was not allowed. The question before us is simply that stated in the resolution: We are dealing with the special privilege which is now given to racing associations under the criminal code of carrying on public gambling operations in connection with their race meetings. I am informed, and I think it is correct, that Canada is the only portion of the British Empire where public gambling at race meetings is allowed by law. If I am not correct, some hon. member will correct me. Personally, I consider this to be a great blot upon our country and a definite menace to our national welfare. The question before us at the present time is a great moral issue, and for that reason it is one of great moment to the people of Canada; for the future welfare of any country must depend upon the character of its citizens. This question, therefore, is of great national importance because it has much to do with the formation of character, particularly in our rising generation.
We find the resolution solidly supported by religious organizations and religious leaders as well as by various other bodies in this country which are working towards the greater welfare of the people and in the interests of social and moral reform. Personally, I have had many letters during the past two weeks from various religious, social and moral welfare organizations in Canada requesting my hearty support of the resolution; and I am told that the same is true of the other members who represent that good old county of Simcoe from which I come. I noticed in the press on Saturday that the churches in the county of Halton have also passed a resolution and have asked the hon. member (Mr. Anderson) who has the honour to represent them in this House that both by voice and vote he support this proposal now under consideration. No doubt a similar situation is true in regard to hon. members of the House generally. Not only is the resolution supported by the various religious, moral and social welfare reform associations, but it is also a matter of very great importance to the financial, commercial and industrial interests of the country. Public gambling at horse races entails, if not the squandering, at least the loss, of vast sums of money as well as the depletion of financial
resources. From reliable sources we learn that no less a sum than $60,000,000 was spent during the year 1924 on the race tracks in this country during the racing weeks, a similar sum having been spent in 1923. Not only that, but as great a sum if not a greater was wagered through the handbook men of Canada during those years. This is a serious condition of affairs and it affects business and industrial enterprises very unfavourably.
I stated a moment ago that this public gambling had an evil influence on character building. Let us not forget that the boys of to-day are the men of to-morrow, and that the influences which are thrown around them in boyhood years are very strong factors in determining what their character will be when they develop into full manhood. Since coming to Ottawa about three years ago to attend the session of 1922, I have personally seen many boys who are employed apparently as sub-agents of those who are dealing in this gambling business. They are engaged selling racing forms and other news articles relating to horse racing, and on two or three occasions, at least on two, if I remember rightly it occurred on three occasions-I have personally been approached by boys in this very city, boys only well in their teens, with the request that I should give them two or three dollars. Now, I have always been personally interested actively in our work with the boys, and I took the trouble to stop and ask them what they wished to do with this money, and invariably the answer was that they wanted to place a bet on some horse in the hope of winning some easy money. I am firmly convinced that the influence of this legalized public betting is absolutely harmful and tends to the weakening of character. And it is a positive menace to our national life.
I have been for many years a somewhat close student of that Book of books which is sometimes spoken of as the guide book of life; and I take it that the same thing is true of other hon. members. From that book we learn that a good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, nor can an evil tree bring forth good fruit. "By their fruits ye shall know them"; and I want for a short time to point to some of the fruits produced by this legalized public betting. For, after all that is the question we are dealing with; we are not discussing private betting that may take place between one and another, nor are we discussing :the abolition of horse racing; we are dealing with legalized public betting on race tracks. In the first place we must remember that the production of fruit is a gradual process. The seed is planted, and after a little

Race Track Betting
while we have first the blade, then the ear and then the full corn, the matured fruit. And just for the reason that the development is so gradual there is a possibility that we may often lose sight of the very close connection between cause and effect. So it is in tlie case of this national evil, this canker which is eating to the very heart of our national life. When we see the fruition of this evil in a ruined manhood and womanhood, let us not forget that it is the ripened, matured fruit of a seed that was sown long before. Let us remember that some influence, some time, somewhere, has dropped as a living seed into that life and produced the fruit which we now behold. I have said that the production of fruit is a gradual process. So it is; and I see it in this light in the question we are discussing at the moment. No young man or woman, when placing a first bet, ever expects to become a gambler, any more than the boy or girl taking the first glass of liquor ever suspects that he or she may become a drunkard. But the result follows; the temptation is there. In this case it is there under legal sanction, and being under legal sanction, these young people are thrown off their guard. The thing is not against the law, they think it is all right, and so they place their bet. Our young men, and young women as well, we know, have done it and they will continue to do it. They majr win for a time and be encouraged, with the result that they repeat the experiment; and they may even win again, and go further into the practice. But the point I make is that this very feature of it, the repetition of the evil, is a habit-forming practice which is undermining the foundation of true, strong character. And when the reverses come; when the fair weather, we might say, has changed to storm; when the winnings have changed to losses, we find that the foundation on which character should be built becomes sand instead of rock, through the process of moral disintegration that has been going on, and the building of true, noble manhood and womanhood falls to the ground.
And more than that is involved. I have referred to the time when losses come, when reverses occur and winnings cease. These losses must be made up. They entail a curtailment, perhaps an entire disappearance of the financial resources of the one who has been engaged in the gambling. And what happens? The need for money is urgent, and he succumbs to temptation. He may be a clerk, or perhaps a manager of some bank or other institution, and he takes that which is not his own; to put it in plain language, he gives way to the temptation to steal. At first it may be
only a small sum, but the principle is the same. That may be followed by larger stealing, often by forgery and embezzlement. Then comes arrest, trial, conviction, sentence, a prison term-all in the trail of gambling. What is the mature fruit of this practice of which we are speaking to-day? It is simply this: ruined character, ruined manhood, ruined womanhood, ruined homes, blighted hopes of wives, mothers and children. I leave it to the judgment of hon. members of this House whether that is good fruit or evil fruit. Judge for yourselves, but in doing so do not forget what I said a few minutes ago: "A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit." If, therefore, we judge the fruit to be evil we cannot get away from the conclusion that the source from which it came is also evil. There is only one course open to us to-day, as I see it, and that is to take such measures as to banish from the land the evil of which we are now speaking.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct the attention of the House briefly to what may be regarded as a case in point. I use it simply as an illustration. Some cases have been mentioned this afternoon by the hon. member for Dufferin (Mr. Woods), but he might have instanced many. These things are actually true and occur in every day life. The case to which I refer took place only within the last month in the city of Hamilton. It is the case of the arrest, trial and conviction of a man in that city-I have his name, but I do not think any good purpose would be served by my giving it. He was charged with theft, conspiracy and receiving, and by Judge Gauld he was found guilty on the major charge; the other charges were not proceeded with. He was convicted on the charge of theft of $31,780 from the Union Bank of Canada. This man was operating a handbook business on a large scale and had been doing so far many months, within two blocks, we are told of the headquarters of the police force of the city of Hamilton. The arrest, conviction and sentence were the result of an admitted embezzlement of a large sum of money from the Union Bank of Canada by a former branch manager of that bank. This branch manager stated during the trial that he had lost all this money of the bank in dealings with this man's handbook in a certain hotel in the city of Hamilton, and also that the man who was operating the handbook business knew at the time that it was the bank's money that was being wagered. Let me quote briefly some of the criticisms that were made by Judge Gauld in dealing with this case, as published in the
Race Track Betting

Toronto Globe under date of February 2 of the present year. It says:
In his judgment Judge Gauld characterized Baird as a shrewd young man, reared since his fourteenth year in an atmosphere of gambling, and one in whom the mercenary spirit was acutely developed.
Just note that one point: the judge states that this man had been reared from his fourteenth year in an atmosphere of gambling- and we have the result, a ruined life. As I said a little while ago, this question is a vital one to the people of Canada because it has much to do with character building, and character is the foundation of the success of this or any other nation. Judge Gauld says further :
It is difficult to find language adequately to comment upon the pernicious evil, in the form of gambling and handbook making, that has eaten its way to such an alarming extent into our community life. The evidence in this case frankly, even brutally, exposed the existence of an illegal practice which has become so common and so familiar that it has been accepted as almost a proper and natural thing.
It has "become so common and so familiar" *-this reminds me of a verse which I learned in my boyhood days while at school, and which runs something like this:
Vice is a monster of so frightful mien,
As, to be hated, needs but to be seen;
Yet seen too oft, familiar with her face,
We first endure, then pity, then embrace.
We see it carried out in practical life. Further the judge says:
Within two blocks of the police headquarters in this city the accused for months has been openly defying the law with his gambling operations. The general impression in the public mind, when thinking of or discussing handbook transactions, is that only small amounts of money are involved, but this evidence disclosed the fact that large sums of money changed hands.
Remember that the sum involved in this case was $31,780. But that is not all that was involved. We have the ruin of the man who operated the handbook as well as of the bank manager who was gambling through him. I think both are at present serving a prison sentence. More than that, Judge Gauld says:
The whole circumstance laid bare not only a wilful perversion of our moral and ethical codes, but a defiance of law and justice with impunity that is incomprehensible to me, and which should require further elucidation at the hands of those responsible for its existence.
When I read, Mr. Speaker, those last few words, "of those responsible for its existence," I just wondered who they were. I know the judge was speaking at the time of the police officials in the city of Hamilton, but after all they are responsible only for carrying out the law, and I feel that we in this parliament are the ones who are responsible. That very thing was what caused me one day last week to ask the government if they in-

tended at this session to re-introduce legislation similar to that which was brought down in 1923, and which was passed by this House but defeated in the Senate, dealing with this identical evil. I was glad to receive the assurance from the hon. Minister of Justice that the government intended to reintroduce that legislation at this session. I hope that when it is re-introduced that it will meet with the unanimous support of members of this House; I hope it will; I hope also that it will be endorsed by the Senate and become law. Otherwise, if the Senate in their wisdom, or in their unwisdom, as I would view it, should see fit to again throw out the measure, they will have a great deal to answer for in the country districts, as I know from actual experience.
In conclusion, I wish to make an appeal to every member of this House for solid support of the resolution which is before us. For in supporting it what are we doing? We are protecting our boys and our girls, our . young manhood and our young womanhood, our homes, this Canada of ours which we ail dearly love, from the harmful influence of this national evil which tends towards the destruction of strong, true, Christian character, and which is also a menace to our future welfare as a nation.

speechtext:
It
was my desire to vote for the main resolution, for reasons with which it is quite unnecessary for me to burden the House, as the matter has been discussed very fully already; but I find that the amendment of my hon. friend the member for Skeena (Mr. Stork) prevents me to a 'large extent from voting for the main resolution. The amendment of the hon. member for Skeena has my hearty approval, and I would like to vote for it also; but I cannot very well vote for them both. If I voted for the amendment, which is a good thing, that precludes me from voting for the main motion, which is also a good thing. That is an undesirable position in which to put hon. members.
I also have one slight objection to the amendment of my hon. friend from Skeena, and it is this, He proposes by his amendment to prohibit the advertising, and so forth, of tips, odds, and so on, unless when supplied on race tracks. Now if it is a good thing to prohibit the publication, advertising and broadcasting of tips, odds, and so on, in any other part of Canada, why is it not also a good thing to prohibit it on the race track? I have the honour to move, Mr. Speaker, the following amendment to the amendment, seconded by the hon. member for

Race Track Betting
Selkirk (Mr. Bancroft). I move that all the words after the word "without" be struck out and the following substituted therefor: and to prohibit the use of pari-mutuels on race tracks in Canada.
If the sub-amendment carries, the amendment of the hon. member for Skeena will then read as follows, and I think it will meet the views of a great many in this House, inasmuch as it will perhaps condense into one amendment the best elements in both the motion and the amendment:
That in the opinion of this House legislation should be introduced during this session to prohibit the advertising, printing, broadcasting, publication, or sale of information concerning any tips, selections, odds or any similar intelligence with respect to or applicable to horse-racing, whether held within Canada or without, and to prohibit the use of pari-mutuels on race tracks in Canada.

I
would like to associate myself with the member for West "Toronto (Mr. Hocken) in deprecating the fact that there has been an amendment introduced at all. speakeroldname: Mr. E. J. SEXSMITH (Lennox and Addington) :
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN

speechtext:
I have no desire to prolong this discussion, but because of the basic value of the resolution, building up as it would the moral standard of citizenship and nationalism, I wish to definitely give my stand on this question. There have been strong arguments for the resolution and also against it, and a repetition of these arguments to my mind is taking up time for nothing.
The question is, is it right that parliament should legislate a business of commercialized gambling? Gambling is not a sport: gambling is a disease. Gambling is a general evil that leads to vicious inclinations, that leads to the abandonment of honest toil, leads to loss of property, loss of self-control and of selfrespect; and laws that encourage this ought to be repealed. Horse race gambling does not differ in any respect from any other form of gambling. If that is so, why should the Parliament of Canada uphold that which is demoralizing and degenerating? Horse race gambling should be dealt with by law just the same as any other. What excuse can hon. members have for not supporting this legislation? We believe in democracy; we believe in an educated and intelligent democracy; we believe that right laws are built upon the foundation of moral pricipals; and if we do not brace up the fundamental principles of right nationalism by law, how can we expect to have a right democracy? For my part I cannot see how any member can frame an excuse for voting against the original resolution and persenallv I am determined to vote for it.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. GOOD TO AMEND THE CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
No doubt many members find difficulty in understanding the precise situation which confronts them at the present time. To my mind the resolution would have been a fair test of the opinion of the House; but the amendment also proposes a step in the right direction and no doubt those who wish to see a betterment of the prevailing conditions as regards betting on race tracks and book-making will be ready to support it. While bearing in mind the saying that "half a loaf is better than no bread" a number of us on this side of the House are at a loss to know what to do. As by voting against the amendment we may be preventing legislation that is very far reaching in importance and personally I feel like supporting strongly the main resolution; but if the Speaker decides that the amendment to the amendment as moved by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) is in order I should think it would meet with the idea of the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) as embodied in his main motion. I do not think this is an attempt to stamp out racing. We have harness racing in the province of Prince Edward Island and its success won for that province the name of "The Kentucky of Canada." Probably the best harness horses in the world have been raised in Prince Edward Island. Race meets take place there during the summer months, and the whole countryside turns out for them. The people spend a nice afternoon
Race Track Betting

and there is very little betting that we know of-certainly there is no public betting, and pari-mutuel machines are not allowed. Therefore I do not think any hon. member has it in mind to strike a blow at the sport of horse racing or the industry of horse raising. At our last fall fair, the pari-mutuel machine was introduced, for the first time in the history of the province. I do not know whether that machine should be allowed in a case where the fair association receives a grant from the federal department of agriculture; it may be that such is done in accordance with the regulations of the department. However I am heartily in sympathy with the main motion. We have yet to hear from the hon. member for Brant in regard to the amendment to the amendment, but if he accepts that proposition I think we can all do the same.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. GOOD TO AMEND THE CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) seemed to be worrying over the fact that he was placed in an embarrassing position. I do not believe it is the first time that motions have been made in this House with the object of placing members in such a position. Whether the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork) did that consciously or not there can be no doubt that is the effect of his amendment. Regardless of any embarrassment I would have no hesitation, in view of the whole situation, in voting against the amendment. While I, and a great many others, undoubtedly do agree with the sentiment expressed in the first part of the amendment-and I am glad to know that the sentiment against the handbook evil is seemingly so unanimous-yet the expression of that sentiment is vitiated, so far as the handbook evil is concerned, by the last few words of the amendment. Therefore for that reason, if for no other, I would vote against that proposition. It seems strange that when a motion, directed against a certain evil, is brought before the House, that we should have introduced an amendment directed against another evil, even if these two particular evils are in some measure related. Yet that is the situation in which we are placed to-day. So even without the few objectionable words at the end of the amendment I would vote against it, not because I do not wish the reform outlined in that amendment, but because it is not a question on which I wanted to vote at this time. My desire was to vote, and to have the House vote, on the particular evil that is mentioned in the resolution of the hon. member for Brant. And that hon. gentleman made it very clear in his opening remarks that he did not want these two issues

confused. We had already had the promise from the Minister of Justice that legislation directed against the handbook evil would be introduced here. We accepted that promise in good faith, and no. matter how this vote goes we expect the government will implement the promise into legislation. The hon. member for Brant, as I say, made it very clear that he wished us to consider these two questions entirely distinctly. I am not going to discuss at this time whether the handbook evil or the pari-mutuel is the greater evil. I know there are those who will declare against commercialized gambling as carried on through the handbook, and yet will not seem to see the evil of commercialized gambling as carried on by the pari-mutuel machine. With what little study that I have been able to give to the question by personal investigation I cannot see that the evil of commercialized gambling is done away with because it has been clothed with outward respectability. I quite admit that if one goes out to the Connaught races, as I did myself a year ago, and looks around to see what is going on to outward appearance it is respectable; but I saw things also, when I was there that forced me to the conclusion that the evil was none the less because outward respectability was evident. To put a pig into the parlour does not make it any less pig than when it was in a pig sty.
Personally I would have preferred if we could have voted on the resolution as it was submitted to the House; we would none of us then have been in the embarrassing position which the hon. member (Mr. Hocken) seemed to think he was in. However, I am not embarrassed about it, nor do I think any hon. member need be embarrassed if he wants to express himself on the original motion by voting against the amendment. If the Speaker rules that the amendment to the amendment is in order we will accomplish all we desire to accomplish in the original resolution; and in that event, while I would have preferred that we should have voted on the original proposition I intend to vote for the sub-amendment. If the amendment to the amendment is not so held I shall certainly vote against the amendment. If that should be carried we cannot, under the ruling of the Chair, express ourselves on the original proposition at this time. Should the amendment be defeated however we shall have a chance to divide the House on the merits of the question, and I shall certainly support the resolution of the hon. member for Brant.

I rise to a point of order. I submit, that the amendment to the amendment as moved by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neiil), is out of order. I base my point of order on the following, paragraph taken from the third edition of May, which reads:
Where the original amendment is to leave out certain words, in order to insert or add other words, no amendment can be moved to the words proposed to be substituted, until the House has resolved that the words proposed to be left out shall not stand part of the question. But as soon as the question is proposed for inserting or adding the words of the amendment, an amendment may be moved thereto.
I submit, therefore, that there is another question before the House which must be disposed of before the amendment to the amendment can be in order, and the nature of that other question is clearly defined by May at page 283. Let me read:
An amendment may be made to a question, by leaving out certain words, by leaving out certain words in order to insert or add others, and by inserting or
adding certain words.
When the proposed amendment is to leave out certain words, the Speaker says, " The original question was this," stating the question at length. " Since which, an amendment has been proposed to leave out the words," which are proposed to be omitted. He then puts the question, " That the words proposed to be left out stand part of the question." If that question be resolved in the affirmative, it shows that the House prefers the original question to the amendment and the question, as first proposed, is put by the Speaker. If, however, the question, " That the words stand part of the question," be negatived, the question is put with the omission of those words, unless another amendment be then moved for the insertion or addition of other words.
When the proposed amendment is to leave out certain words in order to insert or add others-
Which is the case in pcint.
-the proceeding begins in the same manner as the last. If the House resolves, " That the words proposed to be left out stand part of the question," the original question is put; but if it resolves that such

Race Track Betting
words shall not stand part of the question, by negativing that proposition when put, the next question proposed is that the words proposed to be substituted be inserted or added instead thereof.
I submit that according to procedure the question before the House is, as here stated, that these words stand part of the original motion. So that the amendment to the amendment is out of order until that question is disposed of. Reflecting on the situation in which we found ourselves before the dinner hour, I came to the conclusion that something must be wrong, because evidently we had got ourselves into a position which was utterly opposed to common sense in the circumstances. It seemed to me that either the amendment must be out of order or that there must be some other provision in British procedure whereby the rights of the original mover were safeguarded. And my faith in the procedure, so far as debate under British rules is concerned, is very much confirmed by what I find in these references. I am glad to think that the ruling of the Speaker this afternoon was strictly in accordance with the proper procedure, as I was inclined to doubt that at first. Not knowing that there was some other provision to meet the situation that had developed, I thought that the ruling, even if in order, was an unjust one. I am glad, however, to find that the ruling was in keeping with the procedure, and I am more than glad to discover that our procedure provides a way out of such a difficulty. I submit that before any further progress can be made in this discussion, the question must first be disposed of, as to whether the words which the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork) proposes by his amendment to omit from the original motion shall stand as part of that motion, thus reserving the rights of the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) and allowing the House to express its will on the resolution moved by him.

speechtext:
I
submit that the hon. member is applying one set of rules to a set of conditions to which they are not applicable. It is a well known fact that May's and Bourinot's rules apply in this House only in the absence of our own rules. I do not need to go either to May or to Bourinot for information on this subject; I can get that information in our own rules, very ably set forth by our present Clerk. The remarks of the hon. member for Nelson would be applicable to a great extent if-well, in fact, they would be applicable if they were in order, but they are not; they are not applicable to the present situation. The hon. member says that
it would preserve the rights of the mover of the original motion, the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good), if the amendment as moved by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork) were put in the language which he, the member for Nelson, suggests. That is true. It would preserve the original motion if the question were put, "Shall the words proposed to be struck out stand part of the question?" But that is not our custom; it is not our procedure. The Speaker says, "The question is on the amendment;" it is not, "Shall the words proposed to be struck out stand part of the question?" That is followed in some of our provincial legislatures, British Columbia, for example, and it often leads to a great deal of confusion; but it is not the custom here. The vote in this House is taken on the question, "Shall the amendment carry?" That is the question, and if it is carried in the affirmative in this instance the motion of the hon. member for Brant is forever estopped. Let me read from our own rules. Rule 36 states the restrictions governing the moving of motions:
A motion may be amended: (a) by leaving out certain words; (b) by leaving out certain words in order to insert other words; (c) by inserting or adding other words.
Then again it says this-and I am quoting only those rules which are applicable to the present situation:
It is an imperative rule that every amendment must be relevant to the question on which the amendment is proposed.
I do not think anyone can gainsay that my subamendment is relevant both to the amendment and to the main motion.
Every amendment proposed to be made either to a question or to a proposed amendment should be so framed that if agreed to by the House the question or amendment as amended would be intelligible and consistent with itself.
I am in the hands of the House if I have not complied with that rule.

Again:

These are all the rules that have any bearing on this question, and I suggest that I have not broken any one of them. Here is the situation as it presents itself to me. The hon. member for Brant has moved a substantive motion; he wants to do something. What does he want to do? He wants to do away, in his own language, with-
-the special privilege given to racing associations under the Criminal Code of carrying on public gambling operations in connection with their race meetings.
He says it is detrimental to the best interests of Canada; that is his view; that is what he wants to do. That is method number one of dealing with the situation. The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork) does not approve of that method, and he comes along with a suggestion which I will call method number two. He says: "I won't go along the lines of the hon. member for Brant; I will deal with another phase of it, that of what is commonly known as book-making -and he moves an amendment to that effect. Now, six or seven hon. members rise up in this House and say: "I am in a position of embarrassment; I want to vote for both the amendment-it is right-and the motion-it is right; but as the one will substitute itself for the other I cannot vote for both." So I suggest what I will call method number three. It is not a new one; it is not a separate one, but it does not accept the amendment of the hon. member for Skeena in full; it does accept part of it. It amends it; it leaves out what some people think should be left out. Then it also takes a portion of the hon. member for Brant's motion, but in spirit only; it does not accept the language of the original motion in its entirety. I say nothing about racing associations, the Criminal Code or public gambling operations on race tracks. In addition to the portion of the member for Skeena's amendment which I include, I simply say "and excluding pari-mutuels." The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie) asked why I did not insert the whole thing again. The custom here, as we well know, is not to put the motion in the words: "Shall the words proposed to be struck out stand as part of the question?" Mr. Speaker, I started out at six o'clock to say that in British Columbia we had during the last season too much horse racing. That fact is borne out by the press reports, which some hon. gentlemen have no doubt seen, particularly during the last summer and autumn. The matter was the subject of agitations on the part of various public bodies in British Columbia; the situation became so serious that representations were made to the provincial legislature and as a result the legislature passed certain regulations cutting down the number of racing days allowable in the province. The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork) is in the fortunate position of not having a race course in his constituency. He says he has one? Well, he is in the unfortunate position, then, of having one; it is one I personally never heard of. I have two in my constituency. There are three race tracks in the immediate vicinity of Vancouver. The result of all this horse racing in British Columbia has been that the merchants and others have protested that money was being spent in race track gambling which should have gone into the stores and into other business. The trouble with us is that there are no Canadian horses running in British Columbia so far as I know; at least I never heard of a Canadian horse winning a race in British Columbia. Now one of the arguments which has always been adduced in support of horse racing is that racing has a
tendency to improve the breed of horses. Well, it certainly does not do that in British Columbia, because they are not raising any Canadian race horses there which ever win races. The horses are brought from Tia Juana and other American race tracks. When it gets too hot for them down there they come up to British Columbia in the summer time and make the circuit of our province. With these American horses, come American race track gamblers, touts and others who frequent and make a living out of race tracks; and these horses and these men in some way or other manage to accumulate most of the money which is spent on the race tracks, and take it out of Canada. That is why the people out there are objecting to it.
I must say that there are some race tracks in this country where legitimate sport is carried on, such tracks as Connaught Park, Ottawa, the Blue Bonnets in Montreal and the Woodbine in Toronto. If all of the tracks in Canada were as well conducted as these, I do not suppose there would be all this agitation against race track gambling; but, unfortunately, that is not the case, and out in our province, as I have said, there has been a great deal of agitation against horse racing being carried on to such an extent. If the improvement of the breed of horses is left out of the question altogether, we find that the only reason left in favour of racing is sport. Well, I am in favour of sport, and always have been. I have played all kinds of games- lacrosse, football, baseball, tennis, and golf now; I am in favour of all kinds of good legitimate sport, but I suggest that sport is not really the main reason, or any reason for carrying on race tracks in this country. The real reason is the gambling feature, and I defy any hon. gentleman to stand up in this House to-day and say that if gambling was not permitted on these race tracks we would have any number of race tracks in this country. Now if you are going to allow gambling on race tracks, why do you not allow it in other lines? It is true there are among us good reputable citizens who enjoy gambling on the race tracks; there are other reputable citizens who enjoy other forms of gambling. When I went out to British Columbia first, in all the cities and towns everything was wide open. They had faro and roulette and poker and blackjack and everything else running day and night, and everybody was happy. In those days when anybody suggested that these games should be stopped, there were many who rose up against the uplifter and said; Not at all, let us go on in the same old way; we are

all right as we are. But will anyone say that we are not better off to-day with all these games stopped? And I think the same thing would apply to race track betting. I am absolutely opposed to it and always have been.

In the first place, I would have to vote in favour of the pari-mutuels being continued; I would also have to vote in favour of what they call handbook betting, because if I voted for either amendment and it carried, I would have no chance of voting on the original motion
What I intend to do is to consider the matter further. I am in doubt exactly what I should do. I submit that a man may invest his property in whatever way he likes, even for his own pleasure. There is in every activity of life an element of gamble. There is a gamble in trade, there is a gamble in the stock exchange, there is a gamble in politics-quite a number of us will find that out, perhaps very soon.
