speechtext:
Of course you
may cite eases such as the one mentioned by my hon. friend. It may be argued that when you acquire real estate and it increases in value you have gained something without labour; something has come to you as a gift from Providence. Quite true, but the cases are altogether different.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. GOOD TO AMEND THE CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext: In what respect?

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. GOOD TO AMEND THE CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
They are altogether different, because the man who acquires property does so with an end in view; he acquires something tangible and pays for it. He acquires that property for the purpose of deriving a profit and of benefiting from it. He pays for something which is worth something. On the other hand the man who bets tries to get the other fellow's money for nothing. The man who bets does not do so with the intent of losing his money; he does so with the intent of receiving something for nothing.
There is an opinion very much stronger than mine on this subject, and it is the criminal code itself. I submit that the exception made in the criminal code whereby horse betting is permitted and declared legal while all other betting is declared illegal, is at once a challenge to common sense and logic. Why should betting be declared a crime in the criminal code in all cases except when it takes place on the race track or in connection
Race Track Betting

with horse racing? This amendment was introduced into the criminal code in 1910 and 1912. I cannot see the logic of it. I cannot see w'hat difference there is between race track betting and any other kind of betting. Yet section 235 of the criminal eodte provides :
Everyone is guilty of an indictable offence, and liable to one year's imprisonment, and to a fine not exceeding $1,000, who-	[DOT]
And there is a full page of prohibitions which are in exactly the same category as race track betting, but the latter is made legal by law, subject to its being carried out under certain conditions. I submit I cannot see the logic of it.
Now, what is this betting? In view of the amendment made to the criminal code and of the results that obtain, I submit that this betting is nothing else than the exploitation of a credulous public under the benevolent eye of the law. People are protected by the law in the accomplishment of something which the law in a general way declares to be illegal. It is illegal for everybody else but them, and in order to make it legal for them an amendment had to be brought in to the criminal code. Again I say I cannot see the logic of it.
Now, gambling and betting are not new. The place where gambling is carried on to the greatest extent is probably at Monte Carlo. I have never had access to the books, but it is said that the revenues derived from the games at Monte Carlo amount to forty million francs a year. The most important game that is played there, is we all know, roulette. Now, what is roulette? Roulette is a game at which the owner plays against the public with an advantage of 2.7 per cent against the bettor; in other words, when you stake a dollar at roulette you are supposed to receive back a dollar less two cents and a fraction. That 2.7 is the percentage against the man who bets; nevertheless, with so small a percentage, the revenues of the Casino are 40,000,000 francs a year. It is not known that anybody ever made money playing roulette if he or she played long enough. You might win once or twice, or for a week or a month, but it is well known that no one has ever played roulette regularly season after season and come out a winner, because this small percentage makes it impossible for the player to win in the long run.
Now how about the percentage in this case. My hon. friend from Victoria City (Mr. Tol-mie) said that the percentage, according to the Criminal Code, was 5 per cent. I must admit that looking over the Criminal Code

in a hasty way, I have not been able to find the percentage, but my information is that the rakeoff is on the average 10 per cent. Now if the rakeoff is 10 per cent, or even if it is only 5 per cent, how can the public ever hope to win at a game with such a rakeoff when no one can win at roulette where the rakeoff is only 2.7 per cent?
Answering my hon. friend from St. James, I do not know what the people here in Canada think, but I know that in the principality of Monte Carlo these games are considered so obnoxious that the people of the principality are forbidden to play them. They are not permitted to go into the Casino or elsewhere where these games are played, because the authorities have come to the conclusion that it is a bad thing for the people to play at odds of 2.7 per cent. Now if that is so in a country which has made gambling one of its main sources of revenue, would it not be so in Canada, where the percentage against the player is very much higher?
I have tried to inform myself as best I could as to the amount of money that has been wagered in Canada on horse betting through the pari-mutuels for the last three or four years, and my information is that in 1921 there was wagered the sum of $80,000,000; in 1922, SOS,000,000; in 1923, $60,000,00, and in 1924, 160,000,000. Taking that last figure, if you wish, a rakeoff of 10 per cent on $60,000,000 represents $6,000,000 or if you take the first figure of $80,000,000, the rakeoff would be $8,000,000, which is taken from the pockets of the people of Canada. I have just said that it is practically impossible to win, but let us suppose that a few people do win. Has it ever profited anybody? Did you ever hear of anyone who had profited with money he won at the races? I never have. Money got easily is always spent easily; it is thrown away almost every time, and for the man who loses there is no way in which he can gain his money back.
Two years ago, rightly or wrongly it was noticed that I was one of the few members on this side of the House who had voted for a similar resolution. A few days afterwards, if I may be permitted this personal reference, I met on the train coming to Ottawa a very distinguished magistrate whose name I shall not mention now, but whose name I could give if necessary, who told me that in his career as police magistrate it had many times come to his knowledge that men, young and old, had been found guilty of embezzlement or theft just because they had spent money which was not their own at the races. These facts are well known. One has only to open

Race Track Betting
books to find hundreds and hundreds of such cases; they are written in England, where betting is so common. From the United States, from practically all of the states which have passed anti-betting laws, people come to Canada, notwithstanding the opinion expressed by my hon. friend from Victoria City, to try and reap some good Canadian money.
It must be remembered that this motion has nothing to do with private betting. That has always been permitted, and remains permitted by this resolution. Neither does the resolution affect tracks on which there are no pari-mutuel machines; in fact, it does not affect tracks at all, but betting on the tracks. I wish to say emphatically that I am not against horse racing; in fact, I have not heard anyone declare here to-day that he was against horse racing.
An argument has been made against this resolution on the ground that it is an attempt against individual liberty. Well, Mr. Speaker, individual liberty is very much of a sophism and a fallacy. Individual liberty exists only within the limits of the law, and not beyond. Whenever anything is recognized as being unlawful or immoral by the law, individual liberty cannot go beyond that. Now this form of betting has been recognized as unlawful and immoral by the law, by article 235 of the Criminal Code, which was amended about 1910 or 1912. Will anyone tell me what has happened in the intervening years to make that which was declared immoral and unlawful at that time moral and lawful to-day? The principle is the same; it has not been altered. But certain strong influences succeeded in having the law amended. I do not wish to cast any reflections upon anyone, but surely what was immoral ten or fifteen years ago must be just as immoral to-day.
I do not want to speak at a greater length except to say a word or two on the amendment. Something rather unusual happened this afternoon when the ruling of the Chair was submitted to a vote of the House. Perhaps I was wrong but at the time I was not able to understand, any better than I am able to understand now, that the amendment as drafted should come as an amendment to the motion. That is the reason why I voted to have the amendment declared out of order. But this reminds me that there is something strange in our rules of procedure. A motion is placed on the order paper. Everybody has time to examine that motion and to study it. Then all of a sudden, while this motion is under discussion, the rules of the House permit a member to present an amendment to it. Immediately the amendment is offered the 44
Chair is bound to decide whether or not it is in order. I submit that under the rules we have now that is an injustice to the Chair, because no matter how learned or how able the Speaker may be it is, in many cases, an injustice to have questions like this submitted to him for an immediate decision. It is also an injustice to members of the House, who are not all lawyers, who are not conversant with the intricacies of the law; and even if hon. members were thoroughly informed on the subject what could they do in a case like the one which occurred this afternoon? I was of the opinion that the amendment should not be allowed and, although I may be wrong, I have not changed my mind. I think the rules of procedure should be so framed that members would have an opportunity of examining and studying an amendment. There is this further fact to be considered: Hon. members do not read the amendment, it is read to them. Now I submit that under the rules of procedure of a court of justice in any city or in any country the counsel in a case should never be compelled to decide on an amendment to a document without having due opportunity to scrutinize it and study its effect and yet in this parliament we are, and I submit very illogicality, often called to decide points like this.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I intend to vote against the resolution. As long as I am a member of this parliament I will not vote for any prohibitory legislation. We are living in an age in which prohibitory legislation is a fad. Everyone wants to discipline his neighbour but is not so anxious to discipline himself. There is such a thing as the liberty of the subject. I have only been to the races two or three times in my life. Still if a person wants to go to the Woodbine and use has money to bet on the races instead of buying a house with it it is none of my business. We have so many prohibitory laws in Canada that I am beginning to wonder whether this is a free country or not. The country is getting tired of prohibitory laws. A person's liberty is confiscated in Canada in a manner equal to the way in which they confiscate men's liberty and property in British Honduras. Not even the member for Brant can make people good by legislation. Mr. Speaker, I propose to vote for the resolution because I believe it is in the right direction. When I say in the right direction I have in mind that the evil of gambling is inherent in the human race, and possibly further restrictions should be placed upon this evil. I do not vote for the resolution because the people 	,
who honoured me by electing me to this position are addicts to this evil. I am going to vote for the resolution because if I did not I would inferentially be giving the government my support in giving special privileges to certain people in this country- that is my interpretation of it. I would be giving the government a license to grant a special privilege to a certain class and deny it to others. I think that is unfair and that is the viewpoint the government should take in the matter.
Now I said gambling was inherent in the human race. Let a man walk down the streets of Ottawa, or any other city or town in the country, and as soon as the sidewalks are bare he will see little boys gambling with their marbles. That is the first stage of gambling in which they figure. Later on, perhaps, the boy, now grown into a man, will gamble on the Winnipeg grain exchange, or even our ladies will gamble at bridge; and I wonder how far we are going to proceed in the way of legislation before we shall eliminate all the evils which flow from gambling.
I spoke to the mover of the resolution some time ago and suggested to him that he broaden it out. However this is very broad at the present time. One of the reasons why I only wish to say a few words upon this is that I do not think the House should spend too much time discussing these heavenly and ethereal matters and perhaps send us home with a poor Grain Act, or a poor act relating to the Crowsnest pass rates, which might not be sufficiently debated. Rural credits and other important questions might not receive proper attention. I think we might devote our time more profitably to such subjects as these, instead of putting too much time on ethereal legislation,
I intend to cast my vote at the present time, not because of representations made to me, but because of sentiments I have expressed; and I propose to vote for the resolution.

Race Track Betting
reason for opposing it. My main reason is this: I believe that in supporting this amendment we are opening the way to what may be a very vicious precedent. speechtext:
A point of order was
raised and I intend to give the ruling now. First of all in order to make the matter as clear as possible I shall read the main motion, the amendment and the sub-amendment. The main motion reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the special privilege now given to racing associations under the criminal code of carrying on public gambling operations in connection with their race meetings is detrimental to the best interests of Canada and should be abolished.
To this motion was moved an amendment by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork) as follows:
That all the words after "that" in the resolution be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
"in the opinion of this House legislation should be introduced during this session to prohibit the advertising, printing, broadcasting, publication, or sale of information concerning any tips, selections, odds or any similar intelligence with respect to or applicable to horse racing, whether held within Canada or without, unless where supplied on a race track in Canada during the course of a race meeting legally held.
Some objection was taken this afternoon to this amendment and the ruling of the Chair was that it was relevant to the main motion and the majority of the House, on an appeal being taken, decided likewise. The amendment was followed by a sub-amendment by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) reading as follows:
That all the words after the word " without " in the main resolution be struck out, and the following be substituted therefor:
That in the opinion of this House legislation should be introduced during this session to prohibit the advertising, printing, broadcasting, publication or sale of information concerning any tips, selections, odds or any similar intelligence with respect to or applicable to horse racing whether held within Canada or without, and to prohibit the use of pari-mutuels on race tracks in Canada.
Now the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) raises a point of order and his objection is twofold. First he cites May, pages 289 and 290, and states:
According to this authority an amendment like the one moved by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork) cannot be carried without the Speaker putting the question, that the words proposed to be left out stand part of the question.
I may just as well quote what May says on the subject as I think it represents the opinion expressed by the hon. member for Nelson. May says:
Where the original amendment is either simply to insert, add or leave out words, an amendment may at once be proposed to it, without reference to the question itself, which will be dealt with when the amend-
Race Track Betting

ment has been disposed of. The most difficult form perhaps-
And this is the point-
-is when the amendment first proposed is to leave out certain words of the original question, and an amendment is proposed to such proposed amendment, by leaving thereout some of the words proposed to be omitted, and thus in effect, restoring them to the original question, in such a case a question is first put that the words proposed to be omitted stand part of the proposed amendment.
Let me remark that this is the procedure followed in the British parliament, but it is not the one followed in this parliament. Bourinot at page 318 states clearly what the procedure is when there are several amendments:
The Speaker will then submit the three motions in the order in which tlies' are made, and first take the sense of the House on the last.
In the present instance, the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill):
" Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the amendment to the amendment?" If the amendment is rejected, it is regular to move another (provided, of course, it is different in purport from that already negatived) as soon as the Speaker has again proposed the question: ''Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the amendment to the main motion (or original question)?"
As I stated a moment ago, the objection taken by	the hon.	member	for	Nelson istwo-fold. He stated this evening that the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni only reiterates or repeats in a milder form-at least that is what I gathered from his	remarks and that	is	what wasclaimed this evening by some hon. gentlemen who spoke on the question-the principle involved in the main motion, and that, if it is carried, the House will evade the main	question.	As I	have alreadysaid, the	rules of	the House	of Commons will not permit the evasion or the obscuring of an issue. The rules are based on common sense and hon. members will at once see that a case such as presents itself this evening has been provided for by our chief authority on parliamentary procedure, Bourinot at page 318:
When an amendment has been proposed, it is competent for any member to move an amendment to the same. In this case the original question is laid aside practically for the time being, and the first amendment becomes, as it were, a substantive question.
What is the practical effect of this? The hon. member for Brant has moved a substantive motion, putting squarely before the House the principle involved. To this motion, an amendment which, notwithstanding the objections that were put forward, I consider, in my humble judgment, is relevant to the main motion, was moved by the hon. mem-

ber for Skeena (Mr. Stork). A subamendment reiterating, it is true, but in a different form, using different words, the principle involved in the main motion has been moved by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. Therefore, according to Bourinot, the main question is laid aside. It is, so to speak, superseded and the question that will come at once before the House is that of the subamendment. If the members of the House say "aye" to the subamendment, then the Speaker's duty is to put the amendment as amended by the subamendment, and then again it is the duty of the Speaker, after the sense of the House has been taken, to put the main motion. If hon. members are willing to vote for the mam motion, naked, as it were, as it was moved before this House by the hon. member for Brant, it is their right to do so. There is nothing wrong with the procedure, nothing wrong with the rules. The House can dispose of the three questions before it and live up logically to the rules. I hope I have made myself clear. The House will be at full liberty to give a free and unbiased judgment on the question involved.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. GOOD TO AMEND THE CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
I second this motion though it is not at all satisfactory. I must join with other members who have objected decidedly to the course which this debate has taken. I have not had the opportunity in any way whatever of expressing my views upon the motion which was before us
Race Track Betting

to-day. This is a substitute motion. The original resolution has gone from before us under the ruling of the chair as supported by the House, but the present amendment does look in the direction of doing away with one little bit of special privilege. I would have supported the motion advanced by the hon. member for Brant because it struck at a certain monopoly under which one particular group of people, those engaged in horse racing, have a special privilege at the present time in Canada which is denied to other people. Two or three years ago legislation was passed making illegal any sort of betting on a baseball game, or the guessing of baseball results, and that kind of thing. Yet at present one particular group of people, a very wealthy group, have certain privileges in this country which are absolutely denied to the rest of the population. If a man is well enough off to be able to attend a horse race he can there engage in the pastime of betting; if he is not rich enough to go there it becomes a crime that he should bet. That seems to be an absurd situation. Then we have the further situation that we are going to make it illegal to have book-making anywhere else but in connection with horse racing and while horse racing is in progress another bit of special privilege. The House is denied the right to express itself on the motion brought forward by the hon. member for Brant by those who are now trying to claim a special privilege for this particular sport of horse racing. If we are going to legislate in this way I think it ought to be known to the country at large. If laws are devised with respect to gambling let them apply equally. Do not let it be made a crime for one particular group to bet in one particular place and then exalt another group above the law; do not let them be accorded a special privilege and safeguarded in every particular. When this opportunity offers the least we can do is to take away this particular betting privilege and in so doing establish something like an equality in the legislation that is now before the House.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. GOOD TO AMEND THE CRIMINAL CODE
speechtext:
I rise to a point of order. I would ask the exercise of the privilege which I think is provided for in rule 42, page 112, subsection 419, which says:
A motion which contains two or more distinct propositions may be divided so that the sense of the House may be taken on each separately.
If ever there was a resolution which contains two propositions, it is the one before U3 to-night. We have the resolution of the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) who wants to do away with pari-mutuels. We have the proposition of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Stork) who wants to do away with 'book-making off the race tracks. These are the two separate propositions. If we divide the motion and take the sense of the House on each one separately we will accomplish what we have been trying to do all afternoon.

I understand the hon.
member raised the point of order that the amendment and the resolution deal with two separate subjects, and therefore -that the question involved by the amendment is out of order.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURN

speechtext: No, I would not quite take that position. The rules do not quite prescribe the procedure here. It simply says that th-e sense of the House may be taken on each separately. I do not take -the point that the amendment is out of order. I simply ask that the motion should be divided, as it contains two propositions, so that -the sense of the House may be taken.

The paragraph quoted by the hon. member is not a rule. It is only an authority cited under rule 42. The question which the hon. member has in mind I think is that the amendment is not relevant to the main motion. That point has been settled. It has been decided by the Speaker that the amendment was relevant to the main motion.
Being of the opinion that the amendment is relevant to the main motion, I therefore rule that the point of order is not well
taken.
Motion agreed to on division.
